title: Inclusive design in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about disability, accessibility and who designs get made for: in Germany, the UK, the EU and online.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are.

outro.heading: Exclusion is often invisible.
paras: Today's numbers were about who has a disability, how most disabilities begin, who uses subtitles, and how many websites still fail basic checks. The people a design leaves out are often not the people we picture.
Keep those numbers in mind today.

questions.q: What share of people in Germany have an officially recognised severe disability?
questions.explain: At the end of 2025, just over 7.8 million people in Germany had a recognised severe disability: 9.4% of the population, almost one in ten. Most of them are over 55.
questions.source: Destatis, press release, July 2026 (data at 31 December 2025)

questions.q: Of those severe disabilities in Germany, what share were present from birth or appeared in the first year of life?
questions.explain: Only 3% were present from birth; just over 91% were caused by illness. Most disabilities arrive during a person's life, which means any of us may need accessible design one day.
questions.source: Destatis, press release, July 2026 (data at 31 December 2025)

questions.q: WebAIM tests the home pages of the world's top one million websites every year. In 2026, what share had detectable accessibility failures?
questions.explain: 95.9% of home pages failed, with an average of about 56 detected errors per page. Automated tests only find some problems, so the real picture is probably worse.

questions.q: What was the most common accessibility error on those home pages?
questions.sub: of home pages had low-contrast text
questions.explain: Low-contrast text appeared on 83.9% of home pages; missing alt text on 53.1%. Contrast is a visual design choice, often made for style, and it shuts out people with low vision, and anyone reading a phone in sunlight.

questions.q: A 2019 University of Virginia study looked at frontal car crashes. Compared with a man wearing a seatbelt, how much higher were a belted woman's odds of serious injury?
questions.explain: Belted women had 73% higher odds of serious injury, even after the researchers allowed for age, height, weight and crash severity. For decades, the standard crash-test dummy was based on an average man.
questions.source: University of Virginia, Center for Applied Biomechanics, study in Traffic Injury Prevention, 2019

questions.q: Colour blindness affects about 1 in 12 men. Roughly how many women does it affect?
questions.explain: The common red–green forms are passed on through the X chromosome, so men are affected far more often. Red–green colour coding in charts, maps and buttons can make information disappear for them.
questions.source: nidirect (NHS Northern Ireland), Colour vision deficiency; Colour Blind Awareness

questions.q: In a 2021 survey, 80% of UK 18–24-year-olds said they use subtitles some or all of the time. What share of those subtitle users were deaf or hard of hearing?
questions.explain: Only 10% of the young subtitle users were deaf, deafened or hard of hearing. Subtitles were designed for one group, and now help noisy flats, non-native speakers and people watching on phones.

questions.q: Since which date have many new products and services sold in the EU, such as e-books, banking apps, online shops and ticket machines, had to meet accessibility rules?
questions.explain: The European Accessibility Act has applied since 28 June 2025. Germany put it into law as the Barrierefreiheitsstärkungsgesetz, so accessibility is now a legal requirement for many digital products, not just good practice.
